article.headline: Feynman Brings Autonomous AI Agents to Scientific Research
article.lede: A new open-source tool called Feynman promises to do the leg-work of academic research — hunting literature, synthesizing findings into cited briefs, auditing papers against their own code, and spinning up GPU experiments — on command. Its creator frames it as 'Claude Code for research,' borrowing the analogy from Anthropic's agentic coding assistant for software development. Released under an MIT license and installable via a single shell command, it targets AI scientists, engineers, and research teams.
article.body:
The comparison to Claude Code is instructive. Where that tool orchestrates an AI model to write and run software in a development environment, Feynman orchestrates a *multi-agent system* — several specialized AI models, each with a narrow role — across the messier terrain of scientific inquiry. A Researcher agent hunts for evidence across papers, the web, and code repositories; a Reviewer grades claims by severity and flags methodological gaps; a Writer structures findings into polished drafts; and a Verifier cross-checks every citation before the output reaches the user.

The tool's workflows, invoked as slash commands or plain English, map onto the research lifecycle. `/deepresearch` runs a full multi-agent investigation; `/lit` produces a literature review with a consensus map; `/audit` compares what a paper claims against what its released code actually does — a pointed answer to the **reproducibility crisis** that has embarrassed several high-profile machine-learning results; and `/replicate` drafts and executes an experiment inside a sandboxed Docker container. When local hardware falls short, Feynman can burst workloads onto *RunPod*, a cloud platform that rents GPU-equipped virtual machines by the hour.

The creator's demo claim — that the tool returned a **cited meta-analysis** in thirty minutes — is plausible given the architecture. Papers are sourced via *AlphaXiv*, a search and annotation layer built atop arXiv, the preprint server that hosts most cutting-edge AI and physics research. Every output is anchored to a source by design; the Verifier agent strips dead links and flags uncited claims before delivery.

The broader context matters. AI-assisted research tools have proliferated, but most are wrappers around a single language model that can hallucinate citations with convincing confidence. Feynman's design bet is that separating the roles — searching, criticizing, writing, verifying — reduces the chance that confident nonsense slips through unchallenged. Whether that holds under rigorous use remains to be tested, but the architecture at least encodes the right instinct: treat every claim as guilty until a source proves it innocent.

concepts.definition: A software design in which several specialized AI models — each with a narrow role — coordinate on a single task rather than routing everything through one general model. The intuition is that a Researcher agent, a Reviewer agent, and a Verifier agent working in sequence are less likely to produce confident errors than one model wearing all three hats at once.

A search and annotation layer built on top of arXiv, the open-access preprint server used by most AI, physics, and mathematics researchers to share papers before formal journal peer review. AlphaXiv adds question-answering, code-reading, and linking capabilities on top of the raw PDF archive.

A cloud platform that rents GPU-equipped virtual machines on an hourly basis, popular in AI research for running training runs or experiments that would take days on a laptop. Feynman uses it as an external compute target when local hardware cannot handle a replication experiment.

A statistical technique that pools results from multiple independent studies on the same question to produce a single, higher-confidence estimate. Because it synthesizes existing work rather than generating new data, it sits near the top of the evidence hierarchy in most scientific fields.

The widespread finding, documented since the early 2010s across psychology, medicine, and more recently machine learning, that a significant fraction of published results cannot be independently replicated. In ML, a common cause is a gap between what a paper claims and what its released code actually implements — exactly the mismatch Feynman's `/audit` command is designed to expose.
